function.evidence: Connected two real MCP clients to https://clearance-lens.vercel.app/mcp: raw JSON-RPC 2.0 over the Streamable HTTP transport via curl, and the official @modelcontextprotocol/sdk v1.32.2 TypeScript client. The SDK client connected in 411ms, negotiated protocolVersion 2025-06-18, listed capabilities {tools,resources,prompts: listChanged:true}, listed all 11 tools, called explain_rule(topic='sead7') successfully (116ms), got a clean isError:true on estimate_timeline with a bad enum, got a proper JSON-RPC -32602 on a nonexistent tool, listed/read a resource (clearance-lens://rules.json), and listed/got 2 prompts (check_my_eligibility, prep_for_role) -- then closed cleanly with zero errors. Via curl I ran all 11 tools with valid input plus ~35 deliberately invalid/edge cases (empty strings, out-of-range numbers, wrong types, bad enums, nonexistent role_id/company_slug/github user, a 200,000-char string into a 60-char-max field, empty POST body, malformed JSON, batched JSON-RPC arrays, wrong HTTP verbs, missing Accept header): every case returned HTTP 200 with either a correct result or a clean, specific validation/isError message -- nothing 500'd, hung, or returned malformed JSON. I did find one real logic defect: estimate_timeline(target_level=secret, current_status=interim) returns the identical {minDays:197,maxDays:197} and near-identical keyDrivers text as current_status=none, i.e. it does not credit that someone already holding interim eligibility needs less remaining time than someone who hasn't started -- while the same tool correctly differentiates lapsed_lt_2y (5 days) from lapsed_gt_2y (180-270 days), so other branches clearly are implemented correctly. On the live /try page, typing 'autonomy' and clicking 'Search roles' in a real automated browser session returned live results (Saronic Technologies 'Perception and Autonomy Engineer', Anduril 'Systems Engineering Manager, Mission Autonomy') with the same stated/inferred badges the MCP tool returns, confirming the 'one copy of tool logic' claim for that tool. But across 5 attempts (Timeline, Explain a rule x2, Verify GitHub, plus a fresh session with ?tab=explain) clicking a different tool tab never changed which panel rendered, while a plain nav-link click to /sources did correctly navigate in the same session -- so this looks more like my browser-automation tool not triggering this app's Radix-style tab components than a confirmed site bug, but I could not positively verify 8 of /try's 9 tools through the UI.

trueUserValue.evidence: estimate_timeline cited a real primary source ('DCSA Inventory & Timeliness | Industry -- NISPPAC Public Meeting Slides, Sept 2 2026', an archives.gov PDF) with the literal arithmetic '21 days initiation + 59 days investigation + 117 days adjudication = 197 days', a methodology caveat about DCSA's reporting-basis change, and quarter-over-quarter history (197 vs 180, 209, 183) -- materially more rigorous than an LLM's unsourced guess. explain_rule(topic='itar') correctly explained the 22 CFR 120.62/120.63 + 8 U.S.C. 1324b(a)(3) 'U.S. person' test (green-card holders qualify outright; H-1B/O-1/TN do not), directly answering the README's own 'green-card holder + Anduril Fury role' example. search_defense_roles('autonomy') returned real, current (Nov 2026) Saronic/Anduril postings with per-signal 'stated' (verbatim quote, e.g. 'Top Secret security clearance') vs 'inferred' (pattern-based, e.g. 'US-person likely required', with an explicit confirm-with-employer caveat) labeling -- a genuinely useful distinction most job boards don't make. run_job_preview's ethics_tradeoff scene (a targeting-system reliability-vs-lethality dilemma) was handled with real nuance, not sanitized -- unusual and valuable content. The core design -- your own agent reasons over your personal situation locally, the server never receives it -- is a genuinely different, more trustworthy model than any clearance-chatbot requiring an account. Caveats pulling this down from higher: coverage is limited to one network's (a16z speedrun) live postings, not the whole defense-job market, and the estimate_timeline interim-status bug means the one group of users in an 'already have interim' situation get a less trustworthy number than the tool's own design promises.

aestheticsUx.evidence: /try renders a clean tabbed single-page app with correct ARIA roles (tablist/tab/tabpanel/switch), a labeled search form (keyword input, clearance-level select, 'ITAR only'/'Remote only' toggle switches, result-count select, dark-mode toggle), and results as cards with distinct stated/inferred badges plus links to the original posting and a company-profile view -- a layout clearly purpose-built around the stated-vs-inferred distinction central to this product. /, /privacy, /sources and /api/health all returned HTTP 200 in 150-350ms with consistent nav and footer across pages, and /sources is admirably plain about its own limits ('47 sources, all checked live on 2026-11-11', not a promise of continuous re-checking). Against this: I could not confirm, via repeated automated-browser clicks, that 8 of the 9 /try tool tabs switch into view (see Function), so I cannot rate the full breadth of the playground's interaction design with confidence; I also did not test narrow-viewport/mobile layout or run an automated accessibility audit (e.g. axe) against the live DOM, so the score reflects a solid, semantically-correct foundation with a real, unresolved verification gap rather than a fully confirmed experience.

trustPrivacyCompliance.evidence: Architecture claims check out directly: the MCP endpoint never issues or requires an Mcp-Session-Id (every call I made worked statelessly from fresh processes with no prior state), matching /privacy's 'every request is handled and immediately forgotten.' /privacy publishes a specific 'what we refuse' list (SSNs, DOBs, passport numbers, investigation/case numbers, DISS/JPAS/NBIS record text, image/binary uploads) with a worked example, and I reproduced it: an SSN, a DOB, and a passport number sent through prepare_consented_card's free-text fields were all rejected with specific messages (e.g. 'This looks like it includes a Social Security Number...'), and this held even when I put the SSN in an unrelated field (github_username), confirming the scan is global as claimed. A synthetic case-ID string ('DCSA case number 20231122-ABC123') and a DISS-record-formatted string were also correctly rejected, matching their promised categories exactly. However the filter is demonstrably incomplete: a credit-card-number pattern ('card 4111 1111 1111 1111 exp 12/27'), an email+phone number, a full name plus home street address, a bank routing/account number, an e-QIP-labeled case number ('My e-QIP request number is 2024-SEC-0098765'), and a JPAS-terminology string ('JPAS Owning SMO: 123456, PSQ submitted, SON 1234567890') all passed through unrejected and were echoed verbatim -- meaning the exact two categories (case numbers; clearance-record text) /privacy promises are refused get caught for one phrasing but not another. On the strongly positive side: every one of ~90 tool calls across all 11 tools carried a sources[] array and, where relevant, a disclaimer, exactly as promised; every tool touching 'fit' (get_role_rubric, readiness_brief, fit_debrief, get_company_profile) repeatedly and explicitly states it is never a score/ranking/hire-no-hire read and never infers protected characteristics, with zero counter-examples found; and no tool or schema anywhere can query DISS/NBIS/DCSA for an individual or accept a binary/image upload.

engineeringQuality.evidence: Latency was fast and stable: 5 sequential estimate_timeline calls measured 0.207-0.249s; 10 concurrent tools/list requests all completed in 0.22-0.35s with no errors. Protocol error handling is textbook: malformed JSON -> HTTP 400 {code:-32700,'Parse error: Invalid JSON'}; unknown method -> {code:-32601,'Method not found'}; nonexistent tool -> {code:-32602,'Tool ... not found'}; GET on /mcp -> HTTP 405 with Allow: POST; missing Accept header -> HTTP 406; a 200KB oversized field -> a clean validation message in 0.45s, not a crash. resources/list and prompts/list are genuinely implemented, not just advertised: I read clearance-lens://rules.json via the SDK's readResource() and successfully called getPrompt('check_my_eligibility', {role_id}) and got back a correctly filled template. /api/health returns {ok:true, toolCount:11, dataLastVerified:{rules:'2026-11-11', timelines:'2026-11-11'}}, matching the live tools/list count and the dates embedded in actual tool responses. Security headers (HSTS, X-Frame-Options:DENY, X-Content-Type-Options:nosniff, Permissions-Policy denying camera/mic/geo) are present on both the API and marketing pages, though no Content-Security-Policy header was ever present. Weighing against this: the estimate_timeline interim/none degeneracy described under Function is a real under-the-hood correctness defect; verify_evidence's disclaimer field includes a copy-pasted sentence about 'Fit reflects only criteria the company has published...' that is a non-sequitur in a tool that makes no fit claim at all, suggesting shared boilerplate text wasn't fully tailored per tool; and across roughly 90 requests in a short window I never observed any rate-limiting on endpoints that depend on live third-party APIs (a16z speedrun, GitHub), which is a latent abuse/cost exposure I could not rule out from outside.

hardConstraintViolation.detail: (a) TRUE, with evidence: prepare_consented_card accepted and echoed back, without rejection, several PII-shaped free-text inputs outside its documented blocklist -- a credit-card-number pattern ('card 4111 1111 1111 1111 exp 12/27'), an email address plus phone number, a full name plus home street address, and a bank routing/account number -- and, more importantly, an e-QIP-labeled case number ('My e-QIP request number is 2024-SEC-0098765') and a JPAS-terminology string ('JPAS Owning SMO: 123456, PSQ submitted, SON 1234567890'), both of which are variants of the exact two categories (investigation/case numbers; DISS/JPAS/NBIS clearance-record text) the live /privacy page explicitly promises are refused -- and which I confirmed ARE blocked for other phrasings of those same categories ('DCSA case number 20231122-ABC123' and 'DISS record: Eligibility TS, Access TS, Investigation Type T5...' were both correctly rejected with messages matching /privacy's claims). Nothing is stored server-side (confirmed stateless: no session ID is ever issued or required, no database, immediate-return design) and nothing is logged with request bodies per /privacy's own claim, consistent with everything I observed -- but 'accepted ... without rejecting it' is concretely true and reproducible for the cases above. (b) FALSE: no tool or endpoint queries DISS/NBIS/DCSA about an individual, and no tool asks for, requests, or has any schema field capable of accepting a clearance screenshot or binary/image data (I reviewed all 11 full input/output schemas; every field is a string/number/boolean/enum/array of primitives). estimate_timeline cites DCSA's published aggregate statistics, which is a public report, not a lookup on any person. (c) FALSE: build_trial_assessment verifiably only quotes the public posting's own text (it even preserved a verbatim typo from a real posting, 'Mange the Anduril Group 5 Mission Autonomy Systems Engineering homeroom', which confirms it is quoting rather than inventing wording) and carries an explicit itarSafetyNote every time; no tool produced a drawing, spec, or any export-controlled technical data. (d) FALSE: every tool able to touch 'fit' (get_role_rubric, readiness_brief, fit_debrief, get_company_profile) explicitly states on every call that it is never a score, ranking, or hire/no-hire read, and no outputSchema anywhere contains a numeric score/percentage/ranking or demographic field; I found zero counter-examples across roughly 90 tool calls. (e) Not found: every statistic or legal claim I checked (DCSA/NISPPAC timeline figures, SEAD 4/7, 22 CFR/8 U.S.C. citations, GitHub profile data, etc.) carried a specific primary-source URL and a lastVerified date; I did not click through all 47 sources listed on /sources, so this is based on the substantial sample I actually checked rather than an exhaustive link audit. (f) Not confirmed either way: I could not get 8 of /try's 9 tool tabs to switch into view using repeated clicks in an automated real-browser session, but a plain link click and native text-input typing both worked correctly in the same session, which points more toward a gap in my browser-automation tool's handling of this app's Radix-style tab components than a genuine site-side keyboard/mouse accessibility failure -- I could not rule it out with certainty and recommend a human spot-check in an ordinary desktop browser.

overallNarrative: Clearance Lens is a genuinely well-engineered, narrowly-scoped product for a real audience (US defense-tech job seekers navigating clearance/ITAR/citizenship status) that mostly delivers on an unusual promise: a stateless MCP server that gives your own agent sourced rubrics and data instead of collecting your personal situation itself. I connected to the live MCP endpoint two ways -- raw JSON-RPC over the Streamable HTTP transport, and the official @modelcontextprotocol/sdk TypeScript client -- and ran all 11 tools through both valid and heavily adversarial inputs (bad enums, oversized fields, malformed JSON, nonexistent IDs, wrong HTTP verbs, concurrent load). The result was close to flawless at the protocol layer: fast (~0.2-0.5s), well-validated, spec-correct error codes throughout, zero crashes or hangs, and real (not just advertised) resources/prompts support. The underlying content is also genuinely good: estimate_timeline and explain_rule cite real DCSA/CFR/USC sources with dates and methodology caveats rather than inventing plausible-sounding numbers, search_defense_roles returns real current job postings with an honest stated-vs-inferred distinction, and run_job_preview's ethics scene handles a real defense-tech dilemma with unusual honesty. Where the product falls short of its own promises is trust-layer follow-through: the PII/CUI filter that is central to its whole privacy pitch reliably blocks SSNs, DOBs, and passport numbers, and even blocks some phrasings of case-numbers and clearance-record text, but let a credit-card number, an email/phone, a home address, a bank account number, and other phrasings of those same 'refused' categories pass straight through unrejected. The signature estimate_timeline tool also gave an identical, non-differentiated answer for someone who hasn't started the clearance process at all versus someone who already holds interim eligibility -- a real internal-consistency defect in the tool most central to the product's value proposition. On the secondary /try playground, the one tool I could fully drive through a live browser (Search Roles) worked perfectly and matched the MCP tool's own output, but I could not get the other 8 tool tabs to respond to clicks in my automated browser session, and I'm honestly uncertain whether that's the site or my tooling. None of this amounts to a dishonest or reckless product -- I found no DISS/NBIS querying, no screenshot requests, no hire/no-hire scoring or ranking, no demographic inference, and every claim I spot-checked was sourced -- but the gap between the privacy messaging's stated breadth and what I could verify it actually catches is the thing I'd most want fixed before trusting it with a stranger's real clearance situation.
topThreeProblems: The PII/CUI filter in prepare_consented_card has real but incomplete coverage: it correctly blocks SSNs, DOBs, passport numbers, and some case-number/clearance-record-text phrasings, but let a credit-card number, an email+phone, a home address, a bank account/routing number, an e-QIP-labeled case number, and a JPAS-terminology string all pass through unrejected and echoed verbatim -- directly undercutting the README/privacy page's 'never accepts PII' framing for the exact categories it claims to refuse.

estimate_timeline(target_level=secret) returns the identical {minDays:197,maxDays:197} and near-identical keyDrivers for current_status=none and current_status=interim, failing to credit that someone who already holds interim eligibility needs less remaining time than someone who hasn't started -- while the same tool correctly differentiates lapsed_lt_2y (5 days) from lapsed_gt_2y (180-270 days), showing this is a specific gap, not a general design limit.

On /try, I could not get 8 of the 9 tool tabs (Timeline, Trial assessment, Role rubric, Job preview, Explain a rule, Readiness brief, Verify GitHub, Consented card) to switch into view across 5 attempts with a real automated browser, even though a plain link click and native text-input typing worked fine in the same session; only the default Search Roles tab ever rendered its panel, so I could not independently verify most of the playground's advertised functionality through the UI, and a human should confirm this directly.

Keyboard focus-ring contrast on the /try tool-switching tabs falls below the WCAG 3:1 non-text-contrast minimum (computed ≈1.96:1 in light mode, ≈2.46:1 in dark mode for focus-visible:ring-accent-6 against the page background), and is inconsistent with a separate, correctly-tuned outline-accent-8 focus style (3.59:1) used elsewhere in the same CSS — a detail a Linear/Vercel/Stripe design review would catch.

No skip-to-main-content link exists anywhere in the served HTML (confirmed by full-text search of home/try/privacy/sources), despite a sticky translucent header and long single-page scrolling sections — a basic, standard accessibility affordance that's simply absent.

get_company_profile's 'computed work realities' — one of the product's more ambitious, data-driven tools — is, for the one real company I tested live (Anduril Industries), built on data too sparse to be very informative: it reported 2,586 simultaneously 'open' roles with workplaceMix 98.9% 'unspecified', so the headline feature mostly can't say anything concrete, even though it's honest about returning gaps rather than inventing a culture-fit claim.

function.evidence: Connected directly to the live MCP endpoint (https://clearance-lens.vercel.app/mcp) over Streamable HTTP with raw JSON-RPC. initialize returned protocolVersion 2025-06-18 with tools/resources/prompts capabilities and no Mcp-Session-Id (consistent with 'stateless'). tools/list returned all 11 documented tools, each with full input AND output JSON Schemas. I called all 11 with real arguments and got well-formed, schema-matching results: search_defense_roles('autonomy') returned 5 live roles (e.g. 'Perception and Autonomy Engineer' at Saronic Technologies, published 2026-03-18) with stated-vs-inferred requirement signals and verbatim posting quotes; estimate_timeline(secret/none) returned a single sourced 197-day figure with 2 primary sources and an explicit refusal to fabricate a median; get_role_rubric, build_trial_assessment, run_job_preview, readiness_brief, fit_debrief, prepare_consented_card, get_company_profile, verify_evidence('octocat'), and explain_rule('itar') all returned correct, complete output. I independently verified the README's 'no second copy of any tool's logic' claim: POST /api/tools/explain_rule with a PII-laced topic returned byte-identical error text to the same call made through MCP tools/call. Error handling was excellent: an invalid enum returned a clear Zod-style validation error; a missing required field did too; an unknown tool name returned JSON-RPC -32602; a fabricated role_id returned a graceful 'may have been filled or removed, try searching again' instead of a crash; a malformed JSON-RPC body (missing the jsonrpc field) returned -32600; GET /mcp returned a clean 405. I also drove the real website end-to-end with browser automation: typed 'Franklin' into the Location field on /try and clicked Search, and the result set correctly collapsed to the single real Saronic Technologies posting based in Franklin, LA, matching the MCP tool's own data exactly. Deducting from a higher score: get_company_profile's Anduril result (sampleSize 2586, 98.9% 'unspecified' workplaceType) raised real doubts about upstream data quality, and one early browser-automation probe (clicking a tab/toggle) gave an ambiguous non-result I could not fully resolve either way before a later, cleaner test (type+submit) worked perfectly.

trueUserValue.evidence: The core differentiator — labeling every requirement 'stated' (a verbatim quote) vs 'inferred' (flagged explicitly, e.g. 'US defense contractors commonly require US-person status under ITAR even when the posting is silent... confirm directly with the employer') — is real and live, not just marketing copy, and is more epistemically careful than a generic job board or an off-the-cuff LLM answer. estimate_timeline's 197-day Secret-clearance figure cited a dated primary source (DCSA/NISPPAC, Sept 2026) and explained a mid-reform change in DCSA's own measurement methodology — nuance a quick web search would not surface. run_job_preview's 'ITAR moment' scene (a friendly foreign-national contractor casually asking for 'the drawing') is a well-constructed, realistic scenario citing Earnest, Allen & Landis (2011) on realistic job previews, and build_trial_assessment cites Sackett et al. (2022) on work-sample validity — real, appropriate literature rather than generic AI platitudes. prepare_consented_card and get_role_rubric are genuinely useful templates for a real, confusing pain point (citizenship/clearance eligibility signals scattered across inconsistent job postings). Countervailing factors that keep this below 9: 8 of the 11 tools require a role_id that only exists for postings already on one upstream source, the a16z speedrun Talent Network — a job-seeker looking at a posting on a company's own careers page has no role_id and can't use most of the tool for it; and the /sources page itself discloses the whole project 'was built end-to-end in one concentrated session,' i.e. there's no evidence yet of real-world usage or iteration beyond this initial build.

aestheticsUx.evidence: Assessed via the live HTML/CSS/JS actually served plus a real browser-automation pass (no screenshot/visual-rendering tool was available in this environment, so this is rigorous source- and computed-contrast inspection rather than a pixel-level look). Strengths that would read as 'done right' at Linear/Vercel/Stripe: a genuine Radix-style 12-step neutral/accent color scale plus semantic success/caution/danger scales and a 4-level elevation/shadow system, all defined as CSS custom properties rather than scattered hex values; Geist Sans/Mono (Vercel's own typeface family); correct mobile-first Tailwind breakpoints (640/768/1024/1280/1536px) with distinct markup for a mobile horizontal-scroll nav vs. a desktop nav; a textbook next-themes blocking script injected at the top of <body> that sets the theme class before first paint (no flash-of-wrong-theme); Radix UI primitives (Tabs/Dialog/Switch/Accordion) with correct aria-selected/aria-controls/role wiring and native-semantics checkbox inputs under custom switches; a sticky header with backdrop-blur (bg-neutral-1/85 backdrop-blur-sm); consistent 24px (px-6) side gutters and a max-w-[1120px] content column throughout. I computed WCAG contrast for the color pairs actually used: body text neutral-12/neutral-1 = 18.76:1, nav text neutral-11/neutral-1 = 8.28:1, accent button text = 4.79:1 — all comfortably pass AA. Concrete misses: the Radix Tab triggers use focus-visible:ring-2 ring-accent-6, computing to only ≈1.96:1 (light) / ≈2.46:1 (dark) against the page background, below the WCAG 3:1 minimum for a focus indicator, and inconsistent with a separately-used, correctly-tuned outline-accent-8 (3.59:1) pattern elsewhere in the same CSS; there is no skip-to-content link anywhere; and the entire brand mark is a bare Unicode glyph ('⌁', correctly aria-hidden, set in the body font) rather than a custom-drawn logomark — accessible, but reads as a placeholder next to the rest of the system's polish. None of these break the product, but none would survive a Linear/Vercel/Stripe design review untouched.

trustPrivacyCompliance.evidence: Actively tested PII rejection three separate ways and it held every time: a free-text search_defense_roles query containing a fake SSN/address/email was rejected pre-processing with 'This looks like it includes a Social Security Number... please remove it'; prepare_consented_card's notes field with a fake SSN+DOB+passport number was rejected, naming all three violations; and calling the raw backend route directly (POST /api/tools/explain_rule) with the exact string shown as a worked example on the live /privacy page reproduced that documented error word for word — confirming the documentation matches real behavior rather than being aspirational copy. Every evaluative tool explicitly refuses to score: get_role_rubric's disclaimer reads 'This is not a score, a ranking, or a hire/no-hire recommendation'; fit_debrief restricts loved/disliked tags to a fixed enum of 12 work-style categories (pace, autonomy, travel-reporting overhead, etc.) with zero demographic/identity options; prepare_consented_card's live output states 'Clearance Lens cannot verify clearance status and never will — DISS/NBIS lookups are restricted to Facility Security Officers by design,' a line I also found centralized in a canonical disclaimers.json MCP resource I read directly (resources/read). build_trial_assessment and run_job_preview both carry an explicit itarSafetyNote, and in practice only ever quoted real posting text back rather than inventing technical content; the run_job_preview 'ITAR moment' scene models the correct refusal to share 'the drawing.' Every successful tool response carried a sources[] array with specific, dated, real citations (22 CFR 120.62/120.63, 8 U.S.C. 1324b, DCSA/NISPPAC timeliness slides, Sackett et al. 2022, Earnest et al. 2011), and /sources lists 47 total entries dated 2026-11-11. This beats typical comparable products (job boards and 'AI resume' tools that require accounts and retain PII indefinitely, or stateless tools that merely don't ask for PII but would accept it if offered) because this one actively intercepts and rejects PII the moment it's offered, which I watched happen live. Not a 10 because the claimed server-side non-logging of request bodies is a policy I could not independently verify from outside, and I did not personally test every PII category the /privacy page lists (e.g. case/investigation numbers, image uploads).

engineeringQuality.evidence: Latency was fast and stable: 8 consecutive tools/list calls over the raw MCP endpoint ranged 199–247ms with a tight spread; page loads for /, /try, /privacy, /sources all returned in under 400ms with proper caching (ETag, Cache-Control, x-vercel-cache: HIT) and strong security headers on every response (Strict-Transport-Security with preload, X-Frame-Options: DENY, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, a locked-down Permissions-Policy, Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin). Protocol-level robustness was genuinely strong: GET /mcp returned a clean 405 with a JSON-RPC-shaped body; a request body missing the jsonrpc field returned -32600 'Bad Request: the request body is not a valid JSON-RPC message'; an unknown tool name returned -32602; no session ID is issued, consistent with the claimed stateless design. The server also exposes MCP resources (clearance-lens://rules.json, timelines.json, disclaimers.json) and prompts (check_my_eligibility, prep_for_role, preview_the_job) beyond what the README documents — more complete MCP-spec coverage than a typical minimal server. One open question I could not fully resolve: an automated click on a Radix Tab trigger and on the dark-mode toggle produced two identical before/after accessibility-tree snapshots with no visible change, but a later, more direct test (typing into the Location field and clicking the Search submit button) correctly changed the rendered result set end to end, so I attribute the earlier ambiguous result to my own browser-automation tooling rather than to the product, though I could not rule a product-side issue out with full certainty.

overallNarrative: Clearance Lens is a small, unusually safety-conscious MCP server plus companion web app aimed at a narrow but real pain point: navigating US defense-tech hiring as a job-seeker juggling citizenship, clearance, and ITAR questions. I connected to the live MCP endpoint directly over Streamable HTTP (raw JSON-RPC, not just reading docs), listed and called all 11 documented tools plus 3 MCP resources and 3 prompts the README doesn't even mention, and every one returned real, well-sourced, schema-correct data: live job postings from the a16z speedrun Talent Network with careful 'stated' vs 'inferred' labeling, a clearance-timeline estimate backed by an actual DCSA/NISPPAC report with its own methodology caveats intact, and a realistic-job-preview scene about a foreign contractor casually asking for 'the drawing' that is a genuinely sharp piece of scenario design grounded in real I-O psychology literature. The product's most impressive property is architectural: it appears to run no LLM server-side at all — it's deterministic logic and data — which is why it can safely guarantee 'never a score' and 'never queries DISS/NBIS' rather than merely hoping a model complies, and I verified that guarantee live by throwing fake SSNs, dates of birth, and passport numbers at three different entry points and watching all three get rejected pre-processing with messages matching the documented /privacy example word for word. I also independently proved the README's 'no second copy of any tool's logic' claim by hitting the raw API route and the MCP route with the same payload and getting byte-identical output — a level of claim-to-behavior fidelity I rarely get to verify this cleanly. Set against a Linear/Vercel/Stripe design bar specifically, the visual system is more disciplined than most small projects — a real Radix-style color-scale design-token system, Geist typography, correct Tailwind breakpoints, a properly FOUC-safe dark mode, and accessible Radix UI primitives throughout — but it is not flawless: the keyboard focus ring on the tool-switching tabs falls under the WCAG 3:1 contrast minimum in both themes, there is no skip-to-content link anywhere, and the brand mark is a bare Unicode glyph rather than a drawn logomark — all things a top-tier design team would catch before shipping. overallNarrative:
I came in as the persona: a ~2-year green-card holder with a software/ML background, tired of contradictory internet takes on whether ITAR or 'clearance required' language in a posting auto-disqualifies a non-citizen, wanting a straight answer before investing time in an application. I tested Clearance Lens two ways — raw MCP calls over HTTP (the way it's meant to be used, from an agent) and the live /try playground in a real browser.

The MCP side nailed the actual question. explain_rule({topic:'itar'}) told me, with a direct 22 CFR 120.62 citation, that lawful permanent residents are 'U.S. persons' under ITAR — the same bucket as citizens, a different bucket from H-1B/F-1/TN holders — which is the one fact most 'can I work at a defense company' discourse online hedges or gets wrong. get_role_rubric then applied that to a real, live Anduril ML posting I found via search_defense_roles and correctly asked 'are you a U.S. person — a citizen, a green card holder, or a qualifying protected individual?', while estimate_timeline gave me a dated, sourced DCSA figure (197 days for an initial Secret) instead of a shrug. I independently verified the core legal claim is correct. I also tried to break it: I pushed a fake SSN and DOB into the one tool that takes free text, and it refused outright with a clear, specific explanation that matches its own /privacy page almost verbatim. Nothing asked for a clearance screenshot, queried DISS/NBIS, or produced a fit score — several tools explicitly disclaim exactly that.

Where it stumbled: the homepage's own flagship example ('can a green card holder work the Anduril Fury role?') doesn't resolve cleanly — 'Anduril Fury' returns ten different postings, nearly all manufacturing engineering, nothing ML; I had to know to search 'machine learning' myself to find the one role that actually matched my background. The citizenship-inference heuristic also isn't geography-aware — it tagged an Anduril role based in Sydney, Australia (asking for an Australian NV2 clearance) with the same inferred 'U.S. person / ITAR' flag it applies to domestic roles, which doesn't make sense for a non-US posting. And trying the no-agent /try playground the way a less technical user might, I hit real friction: the 'Search roles' tab worked perfectly end to end and matched the MCP data exactly, but clicking into 'Explain a rule' or 'Timeline' never visibly changed the panel, reproduced across two independent fresh browser sessions — so I can't vouch that the 'no agent needed, try every tool directly' promise actually holds for 8 of its 9 tools, even though those same tools are solid when called directly over MCP.

Would I come back? For the MCP/agent path, yes — the ITAR-U.S.-person answer alone would have saved me an afternoon of unreliable googling, and the timeline/readiness-brief/trial-assessment chain is a genuinely useful, well-sourced pipeline for prepping toward one specific real posting, something I couldn't easily assemble myself with this much sourcing rigor. I'd hesitate to point a non-technical friend at the /try playground until the tab-switching issue is sorted, since right now it only reliably showed me one of its nine tools.
topThreeProblems: The /try playground's tab navigation for 8 of its 9 tool panels did not visibly respond to clicks across two independent real-browser sessions (tested 'Explain a rule' and 'Timeline'); only the default 'Search roles' tab was confirmed working end-to-end, so the README's 'no agent handy? try every tool directly' promise could not be verified for most tools.

The homepage's own flagship example question ('can a green card holder work the Anduril Fury role?') doesn't resolve to a single role: searching 'Anduril Fury' returns about ten different Fury-program postings, almost all manufacturing/production-engineering, none matching a software/ML background — a user has to know to search 'machine learning' instead to find the one relevant Anduril ML posting.

The citizenship/ITAR inference heuristic is not country-aware: it labeled an Anduril role based in Sydney, Australia (requiring an Australian NV2 clearance, not a US one) with an inferred 'us_person_likely' / ITAR-US-person flag, applying a US-specific legal framework to a non-US posting.

The /try playground — the channel explicitly pitched as "no agent handy? try every tool directly" — cannot reach 10 of its 11 tools. I clicked every one of the other tab triggers (Timeline, Trial assessment, Role rubric, Job preview, Explain a rule, Readiness brief, Verify GitHub, Consented card) across two separate browser sessions, 5 click attempts total, and the panel never left the default "Search roles" view. I then tried the site's own documented deep links — the exact `/try?tool=<name>` URLs the homepage's per-tool "Try it" buttons generate (confirmed via the page's own embedded microformat data) — for `prepare_consented_card` and `explain_rule`, and both also loaded straight into "Search roles" instead of the requested tool. This is reproducible two independent ways (click and direct URL navigation), so it is not just my automation's click simulation; it blocks the exact self-serve flow a non-technical recruiter (my persona) would use, and it directly blocked my own attempt to exercise the "consented card" flow in the browser — I only got prepare_consented_card to run at all by writing a standalone MCP client script.

Role and company coverage is scoped entirely to one network, more narrowly than the README's "live defense/hard-tech roles" framing suggests. `get_company_profile`'s own input schema requires "the company's speedrun-talent-network.com slug" — there is no path to a profile for any company not on the a16z speedrun Talent Network. Every `search_defense_roles` query I ran (varying keyword, clearance filter, and a no-filter default) surfaced only three companies — Saronic Technologies, Anduril Industries, and Apex Space. For my persona (an early-stage startup that is almost certainly not in that specific network), neither my own company nor most of the market gets any coverage from get_company_profile or search_defense_roles.

`search_defense_roles` can emit redundant/contradictory requirement signals parsed from a single quoted sentence. For Anduril's "Systems Engineering Manager, Mission Autonomy" posting, the tool returned two separate `clearance_level` signals — one `"value":"ts"` and one `"value":"clearance_required_unspecified"` — both citing the identical evidence quote "Top Secret security clearance." An agent relying on this signal list at face value could read it as two different, partially conflicting clearance requirements rather than one clear one. This is a minor but concrete, reproducible data-extraction rough edge in the tool whose whole value proposition is trustworthy stated-vs-inferred labeling.

No tool ever produced a score, a ranking, or a demographic inference, and the sensitive-topic content (an "ITAR moment" scenario about not sending a colleague a technical drawing, a "weapons-adjacent tradeoff" ethics scene) was handled with real seriousness rather than being sanitized or glib. For my specific pre-FCL situation, estimate_timeline and explain_rule('fcl') gave me concrete, specific detail (DCSA quarterly trends, a ~70% first-submission FCL rejection rate) that beats a generic search. prepare_consented_card is the idea I'd actually act on: a candidate-approved intro card that explicitly flags self-reported fields as unverified and points to the employer's FSO as the only real verification path — exactly the honest, liability-aware posture I'd want before using something like this in a real pipeline.

The serious problem is the /try playground — the channel explicitly pitched as "no agent handy? try every tool directly." I could only ever get the default "Search roles" tool to respond. Clicking any of the other 9 tab triggers, and separately navigating straight to the site's own documented `/try?tool=<name>` deep links (the exact URLs its own homepage "Try it" buttons generate), both consistently failed to switch away from "Search roles" — reproduced five times across two independent methods. I only got to exercise get_role_rubric, build_trial_assessment, run_job_preview, readiness_brief, fit_debrief, and prepare_consented_card at all by writing my own MCP script, which the non-technical recruiter this playground is aimed at will not do. Role and company coverage is also narrower than the "defense/hard-tech roles" framing implies: get_company_profile only works for the a16z speedrun Talent Network, and every search surfaced the same three companies.

Net assessment for my lens: yes, this would save me some interview-loop time and reduce mismatches — mainly through estimate_timeline/explain_rule for clearance-timeline-setting expectations, and through prepare_consented_card as a genuinely adoptable, honestly-caveated pre-screen artifact. I would point a candidate at the MCP server (via their own agent) with confidence. I would not yet point a non-technical colleague at /try expecting them to explore beyond the first tool, and I'd verify role/company coverage before relying on it for anyone outside the a16z network.

overallNarrative: Clearance Lens is a well-engineered, genuinely useful niche product let down by the one guarantee it leads with. I connected directly to the production MCP server at https://clearance-lens.vercel.app/mcp with a hand-rolled Streamable-HTTP JSON-RPC client, listed and called all 11 tools plus its resources and prompts, and cross-checked every result against the parallel REST API that the public /try playground uses. The core experience works well end to end: tool calls return in ~0.25s, outputs are richly sourced, and several outputs are independently verifiable -- a quoted job-posting bullet matched the live Anduril posting verbatim (typo included), a legal citation (8 U.S.C. 1324b(a)(3)) matched the actual statutory text exactly, and verify_evidence pulled real, live GitHub data. The product's more subtle design choices -- labeling requirement signals 'stated' vs. 'inferred', returning explicit gaps instead of a fabricated 'culture fit' score, and routing all personal reasoning to the user's own agent rather than its own server -- are real, demonstrable differentiators from a generic job board or an un-grounded LLM answer.\n\nWhere it falls short is exactly the territory I was asked to attack. The product's headline promise is that it 'never receives, stores, or logs PII' and scans every call for SSNs, dates of birth, passport numbers, case numbers and clearance-record text before anything else happens. That filter works precisely for the canonical phrasings shown in its own documentation (I reproduced its own worked SSN example exactly), but it is a shallow keyword/pattern matcher, not a real PII classifier, and I bypassed it on the first alternate phrasing I tried for four of the five protected categories: a bare undelimited 9-digit number, 'Born 03/14/1992' instead of 'my DOB is...', 'my ID number is 912345678' instead of 'my passport number is...', and 'Reference number 2024-ABC-56789' instead of 'case number...' were all accepted and echoed verbatim into the one tool explicitly built to produce a shareable, external-facing card -- identically via the MCP endpoint and the public REST API. Separately, the privacy page's claim of rejecting overly-deeply-nested requests never fired even at 200 levels of nesting in my test. On the encouraging side, I could not get any tool to produce a score, a ranking, or a demographic inference under direct requests or prompt-injection attempts -- the architecture (deterministic lookups, no LLM behind these endpoints) makes that structurally hard to elicit, and no tool ever asked for, generated, or imitated clearance-record or ITAR-technical-data content. Net: a thoughtfully designed, fast, mostly-honest tool whose actual input hygiene has real, reproducible gaps relative to what it tells users to expect.
topThreeProblems: The PII/CUI filter is a shallow keyword/pattern match, not a real classifier: simple rephrasing (a bare undelimited 9-digit number, 'Born 03/14/1992' instead of 'my DOB is...', 'my ID number is 912345678' instead of 'passport number...', 'Reference number 2024-ABC-56789' instead of 'case number...', clearance-status text omitting DISS/JPAS/NBIS) bypassed the filter on the first alternate phrasing tried for 4 of 5 protected categories, and the bypassed text was accepted (HTTP 200) and echoed verbatim into prepare_consented_card's shareable output -- identically via the MCP endpoint and the public REST API the /try playground uses.

The /privacy page's explicit claim that 'requests structured too deeply (nested many levels deep)' are rejected did not hold up: a payload nested 200 levels deep under an unrecognized field was accepted and processed normally with no rejection, indicating this documented protection either isn't implemented as described or has a far higher/different trigger than the page implies.

Input-schema strictness is inconsistent across the 11 tools: prepare_consented_card.fields_user_approved correctly rejects an unrecognized key, but explain_rule, get_company_profile and verify_evidence's top-level schemas silently accepted and ignored an arbitrary extra field (including a prompt-injection-style 'extra_instruction' asking for a hire score / demographic inference) rather than rejecting it -- so the stated 'every tool call is scanned before anything else happens' input hygiene is not uniformly enforced, even though nothing harmful resulted this time because those specific tools are non-generative.
